title: 01. Fundamentals: Fundamentals of Concurrency
summary: Concurrency is about _structure_—designing your program to handle multiple tasks that can make progress independently. Tasks don't necessarily run at the same instant but are managed so they don't block each other unnecessarily.
objectives: When to Use Threads, Processes, or Async

sections.title: 1.1 Concurrency vs Parallelism
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```

║                    CONCURRENCY vs PARALLELISM                               ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  CONCURRENCY: Dealing with multiple things at once (structure)              ║
║  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────              ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Time ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║                                                                             ║
║  CPU:  ┌──Task A──┐    ┌──Task A──┐         ┌──Task A──┐                   ║
║        └──────────┘    └──────────┘         └──────────┘                   ║
║              ┌──Task B──┐    ┌──Task B──┐         ┌──Task B──┐             ║
║              └──────────┘    └──────────┘         └──────────┘             ║
║                    ┌──Task C──┐         ┌──Task C──┐                       ║
║                    └──────────┘         └──────────┘                       ║
║                                                                             ║
║  ONE core, tasks INTERLEAVED (context switching)                            ║

║                                                                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  PARALLELISM: Doing multiple things at once (execution)                     ║
║  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────                     ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Time ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────►               ║
║                                                                             ║
║  CPU 1: ┌────────────────Task A────────────────┐                           ║
║         └──────────────────────────────────────┘                           ║
║  CPU 2: ┌────────────────Task B────────────────┐                           ║
║         └──────────────────────────────────────┘                           ║
║  CPU 3: ┌────────────────Task C────────────────┐                           ║
║         └──────────────────────────────────────┘                           ║
║                                                                             ║
║  MULTIPLE cores, tasks run SIMULTANEOUSLY                                   ║
║  "Actually doing multiple things at the same instant"                       ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Real-World Analogy

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         COFFEE SHOP ANALOGY                                 │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│  CONCURRENT (1 barista, multiple orders):                                   │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
│                                                                             │
│    ☕ Barista starts Order 1 espresso machine                              │
│       │                                                                     │
│       │ (espresso brewing - waiting)                                        │
│       │   └──► Starts Order 2 steaming milk                                │
│       │          │                                                          │
│       │          │ (milk steaming - waiting)                                │
│       │          │   └──► Takes Order 3                                    │
│       │          │                                                          │
│       │◄─────────┘ Finishes Order 2                                        │
│       │                                                                     │
│    ◄──┘ Finishes Order 1                                                   │
│                                                                             │
│    Result: 1 person handles 3 orders efficiently by interleaving tasks     │
│                                                                             │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│  PARALLEL (3 baristas, 3 orders):                                           │
│  ────────────────────────────────                                           │
│                                                                             │
│    Barista 1: ☕ ═══════ Order 1 ═══════ ✓                                 │
│    Barista 2: ☕ ═══════ Order 2 ═══════ ✓                                 │
│    Barista 3: ☕ ═══════ Order 3 ═══════ ✓                                 │
│                                                                             │
│    Result: 3 people complete 3 orders simultaneously                        │
│                                                                             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Plain Explanation

**Concurrency** is about _structure_—designing your program to handle multiple tasks that can make progress independently. Tasks don't necessarily run at the same instant but are managed so they don't block each other unnecessarily.

**Parallelism** is about _execution_—actually running multiple tasks simultaneously on multiple CPU cores.

Key insight: **Concurrency enables parallelism** but doesn't require it. You can have concurrency on a single-core CPU (via time-slicing), but you need multiple cores for true parallelism.

  end

diagrams.explain: **Concurrency** is about *dealing with* many things at once: one core switches between tasks, so both make progress but only one runs at any instant. **Parallelism** is about *doing* many things at once: separate cores execute tasks at the same moment. Threads and asyncio give you concurrency in CPython; only multiple processes (or GIL-free C code) give you CPU parallelism.

sections.title: 1.2 Blocking vs Non-Blocking I/O
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    BLOCKING vs NON-BLOCKING I/O                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  BLOCKING I/O:                                                              ║
║  ─────────────                                                              ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Thread    ┌─────┐                                       ┌─────┐            ║
║            │Work │                                       │Work │            ║
║            └──┬──┘                                       └─────┘            ║
║               │                                              ▲              ║
║               ▼                                              │              ║
║            ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │              ║
║            │  ████████ BLOCKED (waiting for I/O) ████████ │──┘              ║
║            │     File read / Network request / DB query   │                 ║
║            └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                 ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Thread does NOTHING while waiting. CPU cycles wasted!                      ║
║                                                                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  NON-BLOCKING I/O:                                                          ║
║  ────────────────                                                           ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Thread    ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐                 ║
║            │Work │ │Work │ │Work │ │Work │ │Work │ │Handle│                ║
║            │  A  │ │  B  │ │  C  │ │  D  │ │  E  │ │Result│                ║
║            └──┬──┘ └─────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘ └──────┘                ║
║               │                                       ▲                     ║
║               │ Start I/O                             │ I/O Complete        ║
║               │ (returns immediately)                 │ (callback/await)    ║
║               ▼                                       │                     ║
║            ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┴──┐                  ║
║            │    Operating System handles I/O in          │                  ║
║            │    background (DMA, kernel threads)         │                  ║
║            └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘                  ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Thread continues working! I/O happens in background.                       ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Timeline Comparison

```
BLOCKING (Sequential):
Time:     0ms    100ms   200ms   300ms   400ms   500ms   600ms
          │───────│───────│───────│───────│───────│───────│
Request 1 │████████████████│
Request 2                  │████████████████│
Request 3                                   │████████████████│
                                                              │
Total: 600ms                                                  ▼

NON-BLOCKING (Concurrent):
Time:     0ms    100ms   200ms
          │───────│───────│
Request 1 │████████████████│
Request 2 │████████████████│  (Started at same time!)
Request 3 │████████████████│
                           │
Total: 200ms               ▼

SPEEDUP: 3x faster with non-blocking I/O!
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Blocking I/O (BAD for concurrency)

```python
import time
import requests

def fetch_url_blocking(url):
    """Blocking: Thread waits for response"""
    print(f"Starting request to {url}")
    response = requests.get(url)  # BLOCKS here!
    print(f"Got response from {url}: {len(response.content)} bytes")
    return response

# Sequential execution - each request blocks
start = time.time()
urls = [
    "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
    "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
    "https://httpbin.org/delay/1"
]

for url in urls:
    fetch_url_blocking(url)

print(f"Total time (blocking): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
# Output: ~3 seconds (each request waits for previous)
```

#### Example 2: Non-Blocking I/O with asyncio

```python
import asyncio
import aiohttp
import time

async def fetch_url_nonblocking(session, url):
    """Non-blocking: Coroutine yields control while waiting"""
    print(f"Starting request to {url}")
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        content = await response.read()  # Yields control here!
        print(f"Got response from {url}: {len(content)} bytes")
        return content

async def main():
    start = time.time()
    urls = [
        "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
        "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
        "https://httpbin.org/delay/1"
    ]

    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        # All requests start at the same time!
        tasks = [fetch_url_nonblocking(session, url) for url in urls]
        await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    print(f"Total time (non-blocking): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Output: ~1 second (all requests run concurrently)

asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 3: Simulating Blocking vs Non-Blocking

```python
import asyncio
import time

# Simulated I/O operations
def blocking_io_simulation():
    """Simulates blocking I/O - thread sleeps"""
    time.sleep(1)  # BLOCKS the thread completely
    return "Data from blocking I/O"

async def nonblocking_io_simulation():
    """Simulates non-blocking I/O - yields control"""
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Yields control to event loop
    return "Data from non-blocking I/O"

# BLOCKING version
def run_blocking():
    start = time.time()
    results = []
    for i in range(5):
        results.append(blocking_io_simulation())
    print(f"Blocking: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~5 seconds
    return results

# NON-BLOCKING version
async def run_nonblocking():
    start = time.time()
    tasks = [nonblocking_io_simulation() for _ in range(5)]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(f"Non-blocking: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~1 second
    return results

# Compare
run_blocking()
asyncio.run(run_nonblocking())
```

diagrams.title: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App as Your code
  participant OS as OS / network
  Note over App,OS: Blocking call
  App->>OS: recv() on socket
  Note over App: thread is parked, does nothing
  OS-->>App: data arrives after 200 ms
  Note over App,OS: Non-blocking call
  App->>OS: register socket for read readiness
  App->>App: run other tasks meanwhile
  OS-->>App: socket is ready
  App->>OS: recv() returns immediately with data
diagrams.explain: A **blocking** call parks the calling thread until the operation completes, so that thread can do nothing else for the whole wait. A **non-blocking** call only *registers interest* and returns at once; the OS later reports readiness and the program reads the data without waiting. asyncio is built on the non-blocking style: the event loop waits for many sockets at once with `select/epoll/kqueue`.

sections.title: 1.3 I/O-Bound vs CPU-Bound Workloads
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                     I/O-BOUND vs CPU-BOUND                                  ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  I/O-BOUND TASK: Spends most time WAITING for external resources            ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────               ║
║                                                                             ║
║  CPU Usage:     ▁▁██▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁██▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁██▁▁                           ║
║                   │             │             │                             ║
║                   │   WAITING   │   WAITING   │                             ║
║                   │  for disk   │  for network│                             ║
║                   │             │             │                             ║
║  Examples:                                                                  ║
║    • Reading/writing files                                                  ║
║    • Network requests (HTTP, database queries)                              ║
║    • User input                                                             ║
║    • Waiting for external APIs                                              ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Best approach: Threading or AsyncIO (many tasks can wait simultaneously)   ║
║                                                                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  CPU-BOUND TASK: Spends most time COMPUTING (using CPU)                     ║
║  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────                     ║
║                                                                             ║
║  CPU Usage:     ████████████████████████████████████████                    ║
║                 ▲                                      ▲                    ║
║                 │      CPU at 100% utilization        │                    ║
║                 │                                      │                    ║
║  Examples:                                                                  ║
║    • Mathematical calculations                                              ║
║    • Image/video processing                                                 ║
║    • Data compression/encryption                                            ║
║    • Machine learning training                                              ║
║    • Parsing large datasets                                                 ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Best approach: Multiprocessing (use multiple CPU cores)                    ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Decision Matrix

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        WHICH APPROACH TO USE?                                 │
├───────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────┬───────────────────┤
│    Workload       │    Threading     │   Multiprocessing │     AsyncIO       │
├───────────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ I/O-bound         │      ✓ GOOD      │     ✗ Overkill    │    ✓✓ BEST        │
│ (few tasks)       │   Simple to use  │   Process overhead│   Slight learning │
│                   │                  │                   │      curve        │
├───────────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ I/O-bound         │     ✓ OK         │     ✗ Overkill    │    ✓✓ BEST        │
│ (many tasks)      │  Memory per      │   Process overhead│   Scales to       │
│                   │  thread adds up  │                   │   thousands       │
├───────────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ CPU-bound         │     ✗ BAD        │    ✓✓ BEST        │     ✗ BAD         │
│                   │   GIL blocks     │   True parallel   │   Still single-   │
│                   │   parallelism    │   execution       │   threaded        │
├───────────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────┤
│ Mixed             │     ✓ OK         │     ✓ OK          │ ✓ + run_in_exec   │
│ I/O + CPU         │                  │                   │     rator         │
└───────────────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────┴───────────────────┘
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: I/O-Bound Task Detection

```python
import time
import cProfile
import pstats
import io

def io_bound_task():
    """Simulates I/O-bound work"""
    # Network call simulation
    time.sleep(0.1)  # Waiting for response
    data = "response"
    # Minimal processing
    return data.upper()

def cpu_bound_task():
    """Simulates CPU-bound work"""
    # Heavy computation
    result = 0
    for i in range(10_000_000):
        result += i * i
    return result

# Profile to see CPU time vs wall time
def profile_task(func, name):
    pr = cProfile.Profile()
    pr.enable()

    start_wall = time.time()
    func()
    wall_time = time.time() - start_wall

    pr.disable()

    # Get CPU time from profile
    stats = pstats.Stats(pr)
    cpu_time = sum(stat[2] for stat in stats.stats.values())  # tottime

    print(f"\n{name}:")
    print(f"  Wall time: {wall_time:.3f}s")
    print(f"  CPU time:  {cpu_time:.3f}s")
    print(f"  Ratio:     {cpu_time/wall_time:.1%} CPU utilization")

    if cpu_time/wall_time < 0.5:
        print("  → I/O-BOUND (low CPU utilization)")
    else:
        print("  → CPU-BOUND (high CPU utilization)")

profile_task(io_bound_task, "I/O-Bound Task")
profile_task(cpu_bound_task, "CPU-Bound Task")
```

#### Example 2: Wrong Approach vs Right Approach

```python
import threading
import multiprocessing
import asyncio
import time

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# WRONG: Using threading for CPU-bound task (GIL limits parallelism)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def cpu_work(n):
    """CPU-intensive: calculate sum of squares"""
    return sum(i*i for i in range(n))

def threading_cpu_bound():
    """BAD: Threads don't speed up CPU-bound work in Python"""
    start = time.time()
    threads = []
    for _ in range(4):
        t = threading.Thread(target=cpu_work, args=(5_000_000,))
        threads.append(t)
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    print(f"Threading (CPU-bound): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Still slow! GIL prevents parallel execution

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# RIGHT: Using multiprocessing for CPU-bound task
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def multiprocessing_cpu_bound():
    """GOOD: Processes run on separate cores"""
    start = time.time()
    with multiprocessing.Pool(4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(cpu_work, [5_000_000] * 4)
    print(f"Multiprocessing (CPU-bound): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Much faster! True parallel execution

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# WRONG: Using multiprocessing for I/O-bound task (wasteful)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def io_work(seconds):
    """I/O-intensive: wait for external resource"""
    time.sleep(seconds)
    return "done"

def multiprocessing_io_bound():
    """BAD: Process overhead for simple I/O is wasteful"""
    start = time.time()
    with multiprocessing.Pool(4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(io_work, [0.5] * 4)
    print(f"Multiprocessing (I/O-bound): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Works but wasteful - each process uses significant memory

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# RIGHT: Using asyncio for I/O-bound task
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def async_io_work(seconds):
    """I/O-intensive with async"""
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
    return "done"

async def asyncio_io_bound():
    """GOOD: Single thread handles many I/O operations"""
    start = time.time()
    tasks = [async_io_work(0.5) for _ in range(100)]  # 100 concurrent!
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(f"AsyncIO (I/O-bound, 100 tasks): {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Fast and memory efficient!

# Run comparisons
if __name__ == "__main__":
    threading_cpu_bound()
    multiprocessing_cpu_bound()
    multiprocessing_io_bound()
    asyncio.run(asyncio_io_bound())
```

#### Example 3: Identifying Workload Type in Real Code

```python
"""
Real-world example: Image processing pipeline
Shows how to identify and handle mixed workloads
"""
import time
import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from typing import List
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ImageTask:
    url: str
    processing_type: str

# Simulated functions
def download_image(url: str) -> bytes:
    """I/O-BOUND: Network request"""
    time.sleep(0.1)  # Simulates network delay
    return b"image_data"

def apply_filter(image_data: bytes) -> bytes:
    """CPU-BOUND: Heavy image processing"""
    # Simulate CPU-intensive work
    _ = sum(i*i for i in range(1_000_000))
    return b"processed_data"

def save_to_storage(image_data: bytes, filename: str) -> str:
    """I/O-BOUND: Disk write"""
    time.sleep(0.05)  # Simulates disk I/O
    return f"saved_{filename}"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# OPTIMAL APPROACH: Use right tool for each step
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def process_image_optimal(url: str, executor: ProcessPoolExecutor):
    """
    Hybrid approach:
    - AsyncIO for I/O-bound (download, save)
    - ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound (filter)
    """
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()

    # Step 1: Download (I/O-bound) - use asyncio
    # In real code: async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
    image_data = await loop.run_in_executor(None, download_image, url)

    # Step 2: Process (CPU-bound) - use process pool
    processed = await loop.run_in_executor(executor, apply_filter, image_data)

    # Step 3: Save (I/O-bound) - use asyncio
    result = await loop.run_in_executor(None, save_to_storage, processed, url)

    return result

async def main():
    urls = [f"http://example.com/image_{i}.jpg" for i in range(10)]

    start = time.time()

    # Use ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        tasks = [process_image_optimal(url, executor) for url in urls]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    print(f"Processed {len(results)} images in {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    print("Used: AsyncIO (I/O) + ProcessPool (CPU) = Optimal!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

diagrams.title: Where the time goes: I/O-bound vs CPU-bound
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TB
  subgraph IO["I/O-bound request — mostly waiting"]
    direction LR
    i1["CPU 2 ms"] --> i2["wait for DB 80 ms"] --> i3["CPU 1 ms"] --> i4["wait for API 120 ms"] --> i5["CPU 2 ms"]
  end
  subgraph CPU["CPU-bound job — mostly computing"]
    direction LR
    c1["parse 300 ms"] --> c2["transform 900 ms"] --> c3["compress 400 ms"]
  end
  IO --> fix1["Overlap the waits: threads or asyncio"]
  CPU --> fix2["Add cores: multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutor"]
diagrams.explain: Profile first: if most of the wall-clock time is spent **waiting** (network, disk, database), the work is I/O-bound and you speed it up by overlapping the waits. If most of the time is spent **computing**, it is CPU-bound and only more cores help — which in CPython means more processes, because the GIL lets just one thread execute Python bytecode at a time.

sections.title: 1.4 The Python GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    PYTHON'S GLOBAL INTERPRETER LOCK (GIL)                   ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  What is the GIL?                                                           ║
║  ────────────────                                                           ║
║  A mutex that protects access to Python objects, preventing multiple        ║
║  native threads from executing Python bytecode at once.                     ║
║                                                                             ║
║                          ┌─────────────────┐                                ║
║                          │       GIL       │                                ║
║                          │   (one lock)    │                                ║
║                          └────────┬────────┘                                ║
║                                   │                                         ║
║            ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐                  ║
║            │                      │                      │                  ║

║     │ (wants   │           │ (wants   │           │ (wants   │             ║
║     │  to run) │           │  to run) │           │  to run) │             ║
║     └──────────┘           └──────────┘           └──────────┘             ║
║            │                      │                      │                  ║
║            │     ONLY ONE CAN HOLD THE GIL AT A TIME    │                  ║
║            │                      │                      │                  ║
║                                                                             ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  GIL in Action (CPU-bound work):                                            ║
║  ────────────────────────────────                                           ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Time ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►         ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Thread 1: ██████░░░░░░██████░░░░░░██████░░░░░░██████                       ║

║  ░░ = Waiting for GIL                                                       ║

║                                                                             ║

║                                                                             ║
║  GIL Released During I/O:                                                   ║

║                                                                             ║

║                                                                             ║

║               │                 │                                           ║
║               │ (waiting for    │                                           ║
║               │  network I/O    │                                           ║
║               │  GIL RELEASED!) │                                           ║
║                                                                             ║
║  Thread 2: ░░██████████████████░░                                           ║
║              │                 │                                            ║
║              │ Can run while   │                                            ║
║              │ Thread 1 waits! │                                            ║
║                                                                             ║

║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Why the GIL Exists

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         WHY DOES PYTHON HAVE A GIL?                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│  1. MEMORY MANAGEMENT SAFETY                                                 │
│     Python uses reference counting for garbage collection.                   │
│     Without GIL, multiple threads could corrupt reference counts.           │
│                                                                              │
│     object.refcount = 5                                                      │
│                                                                              │
│     Thread 1: refcount += 1   ─┐                                            │
│                                 ├─► Race condition! Could lose updates       │
│     Thread 2: refcount -= 1   ─┘                                            │
│                                                                              │
│  2. SIMPLICITY                                                               │
│     Makes C extension writing much simpler.                                  │
│     Many Python libraries rely on this simplicity.                          │
│                                                                              │
│  3. SINGLE-THREADED PERFORMANCE                                              │
│     No locking overhead for single-threaded code.                           │
│     Most Python programs are single-threaded.                               │
│                                                                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                         WHAT RELEASES THE GIL?                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│  ✓ I/O operations (file, network, database)                                │
│  ✓ time.sleep()                                                             │
│  ✓ NumPy operations (releases GIL during computation)                       │
│  ✓ Some C extensions (explicitly release GIL)                               │
│  ✓ Waiting on locks, conditions, etc.                                       │
│                                                                              │
│  ✗ Pure Python computation (always holds GIL)                               │
│  ✗ String operations                                                        │
│  ✗ List/dict operations                                                     │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Demonstrating GIL Effect on CPU-bound Work

```python
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time

def cpu_intensive(n):
    """Pure Python CPU work - holds GIL"""
    count = 0
    for i in range(n):
        count += i * i
    return count

def benchmark_sequential():
    """Baseline: run sequentially"""
    start = time.time()
    cpu_intensive(20_000_000)
    cpu_intensive(20_000_000)
    return time.time() - start

def benchmark_threading():
    """Threading: limited by GIL for CPU work"""
    start = time.time()
    t1 = threading.Thread(target=cpu_intensive, args=(20_000_000,))
    t2 = threading.Thread(target=cpu_intensive, args=(20_000_000,))
    t1.start()
    t2.start()
    t1.join()
    t2.join()
    return time.time() - start

def benchmark_multiprocessing():
    """Multiprocessing: bypasses GIL"""
    start = time.time()
    with multiprocessing.Pool(2) as pool:
        pool.map(cpu_intensive, [20_000_000, 20_000_000])
    return time.time() - start

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("CPU-bound work benchmark:")
    print("-" * 40)

    seq_time = benchmark_sequential()
    print(f"Sequential:      {seq_time:.2f}s (baseline)")

    thread_time = benchmark_threading()
    print(f"Threading:       {thread_time:.2f}s ({seq_time/thread_time:.1f}x)")
    print("  └─ No speedup! GIL prevents parallel execution")

    mp_time = benchmark_multiprocessing()
    print(f"Multiprocessing: {mp_time:.2f}s ({seq_time/mp_time:.1f}x)")
    print("  └─ ~2x speedup! Processes bypass GIL")
```

Output:

```
CPU-bound work benchmark:
----------------------------------------
Sequential:      4.52s (baseline)
Threading:       4.67s (1.0x)
  └─ No speedup! GIL prevents parallel execution
Multiprocessing: 2.31s (2.0x)
  └─ ~2x speedup! Processes bypass GIL
```

#### Example 2: GIL Released During I/O

```python
import threading
import time
import requests

def io_task(url):
    """I/O-bound: GIL is released during network wait"""
    response = requests.get(url)
    return len(response.content)

def benchmark_io_sequential():
    """Sequential I/O"""
    start = time.time()
    urls = ["https://httpbin.org/delay/1"] * 4
    for url in urls:
        io_task(url)
    return time.time() - start

def benchmark_io_threading():
    """Threaded I/O - GIL released during wait"""
    start = time.time()
    threads = []
    urls = ["https://httpbin.org/delay/1"] * 4

    for url in urls:
        t = threading.Thread(target=io_task, args=(url,))
        threads.append(t)
        t.start()

    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    return time.time() - start

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("I/O-bound work benchmark:")
    print("-" * 40)

    seq_time = benchmark_io_sequential()
    print(f"Sequential: {seq_time:.2f}s")

    thread_time = benchmark_io_threading()
    print(f"Threading:  {thread_time:.2f}s ({seq_time/thread_time:.1f}x speedup!)")
    print("  └─ Threading WORKS for I/O! GIL released during wait.")
```

#### Example 3: Checking if GIL is Released (sys.getswitchinterval)

```python
import sys
import threading
import time

# Check GIL switch interval (how often threads get a chance to run)
print(f"GIL switch interval: {sys.getswitchinterval()} seconds")
# Default is 0.005 seconds (5ms)

# You can change it (not recommended for most cases)
# sys.setswitchinterval(0.001)  # Switch more frequently

def counter_without_gil_awareness():
    """
    This demonstrates why you need locks even with GIL.
    GIL doesn't make your code thread-safe!
    """
    global shared_counter
    for _ in range(100000):
        # This is NOT atomic! GIL can switch between:
        # 1. Read shared_counter
        # 2. Add 1
        # 3. Write back
        shared_counter += 1

shared_counter = 0
threads = [threading.Thread(target=counter_without_gil_awareness) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(f"Expected: 400000, Got: {shared_counter}")
print("GIL doesn't guarantee atomic operations!")

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CORRECT way: use a lock
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

lock = threading.Lock()
shared_counter = 0

def counter_with_lock():
    global shared_counter
    for _ in range(100000):
        with lock:
            shared_counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=counter_with_lock) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(f"With lock - Expected: 400000, Got: {shared_counter}")
```

diagrams.title: How the GIL is handed between threads
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant T1 as Thread 1
  participant G as GIL
  participant T2 as Thread 2
  T1->>G: acquire
  Note over T1: runs Python bytecode
  T2->>G: wants the GIL, sets drop request
  Note over T1,T2: after switch interval of about 5 ms
  T1->>G: release at a safe point
  G->>T2: T2 acquires
  Note over T2: runs Python bytecode
  T2->>G: release before blocking I/O
  G->>T1: T1 acquires while T2 waits on the socket
diagrams.explain: The GIL is a mutex inside CPython: a thread must hold it to execute bytecode. A waiting thread asks for it, and the running thread drops it after the **switch interval** (`sys.getswitchinterval()`, 5 ms by default) or immediately when it starts **blocking I/O**. That is why threads overlap I/O well but CPU-bound threads take turns instead of running in parallel.

### Comparison Table

│    Feature       │   Threading    │ Multiprocessing │      AsyncIO       │
├──────────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ Memory sharing   │ ✓ Shared       │ ✗ Separate      │ ✓ Shared           │
│ Memory overhead  │ ~8KB/thread    │ ~30MB/process   │ ~1KB/coroutine     │
│ CPU parallelism  │ ✗ GIL blocks   │ ✓ True parallel │ ✗ Single thread    │

└──────────────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────────────┘

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Same Task, Three Approaches

```python
"""
Task: Download and process 10 web pages
Comparing all three approaches
"""
import threading
import multiprocessing
import asyncio
import aiohttp
import requests
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

URLS = [f"https://httpbin.org/delay/0.5?id={i}" for i in range(10)]

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# APPROACH 1: Threading
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def fetch_threading(url):
    response = requests.get(url)
    return len(response.content)

def run_threading():
    start = time.time()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(fetch_threading, URLS))
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Threading:       {elapsed:.2f}s | Results: {len(results)}")
    return elapsed

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# APPROACH 2: Multiprocessing (overkill for this I/O task!)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def fetch_multiprocessing(url):
    response = requests.get(url)
    return len(response.content)

def run_multiprocessing():
    start = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(fetch_multiprocessing, URLS))
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Multiprocessing: {elapsed:.2f}s | Results: {len(results)}")
    return elapsed

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# APPROACH 3: AsyncIO (best for I/O!)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def fetch_async(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        content = await response.read()
        return len(content)

async def run_asyncio():
    start = time.time()
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [fetch_async(session, url) for url in URLS]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"AsyncIO:         {elapsed:.2f}s | Results: {len(results)}")
    return elapsed

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# RUN COMPARISON
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 50)
    print("I/O-Bound Task: Fetching 10 web pages")
    print("=" * 50)

    t1 = run_threading()
    t2 = run_multiprocessing()
    t3 = asyncio.run(run_asyncio())

    print("-" * 50)
    print(f"Winner: AsyncIO (lowest overhead for I/O)")
```

#### Example 2: CPU-Bound Task Comparison

```python
"""
Task: Calculate prime numbers
Comparing approaches for CPU-bound work
"""
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

def is_prime(n):
    """CPU-intensive prime check"""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
    return True

def count_primes_in_range(start_end):
    """Count primes in a range"""
    start, end = start_end
    return sum(1 for n in range(start, end) if is_prime(n))

# Divide work into chunks
RANGES = [(i * 250000, (i + 1) * 250000) for i in range(4)]

def run_sequential():
    start = time.time()
    results = [count_primes_in_range(r) for r in RANGES]
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Sequential:      {elapsed:.2f}s | Primes: {sum(results)}")
    return elapsed

def run_threading():
    start = time.time()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(count_primes_in_range, RANGES))
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Threading:       {elapsed:.2f}s | Primes: {sum(results)}")
    return elapsed

def run_multiprocessing():
    start = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(count_primes_in_range, RANGES))
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Multiprocessing: {elapsed:.2f}s | Primes: {sum(results)}")
    return elapsed

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 50)
    print("CPU-Bound Task: Counting primes up to 1,000,000")
    print("=" * 50)

    t1 = run_sequential()
    t2 = run_threading()
    t3 = run_multiprocessing()

    print("-" * 50)
    print(f"Threading speedup: {t1/t2:.1f}x (limited by GIL)")
    print(f"Multiprocessing speedup: {t1/t3:.1f}x (true parallelism)")
    print(f"Winner: Multiprocessing for CPU-bound work!")
```

#### Example 3: Hybrid Approach (Mixed Workload)

```python
"""
Real-world scenario: Download images and resize them
- Download = I/O-bound (use threading/asyncio)
- Resize = CPU-bound (use multiprocessing)
"""
import asyncio
import aiohttp
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from PIL import Image
import io

async def download_image(session, url):
    """I/O-bound: async download"""
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        return await response.read()

def resize_image(image_data):
    """CPU-bound: image processing"""
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_data))
    resized = img.resize((100, 100))
    output = io.BytesIO()
    resized.save(output, format='PNG')
    return output.getvalue()

async def process_image(session, url, executor):
    """Hybrid: async download + process pool resize"""
    # I/O-bound: download with asyncio
    image_data = await download_image(session, url)

    # CPU-bound: resize with process pool
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    resized = await loop.run_in_executor(executor, resize_image, image_data)

    return len(resized)

async def main():
    # Sample image URLs (placeholder)
    urls = [
        "https://picsum.photos/1000/1000"
        for _ in range(10)
    ]

    start = time.time()

    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
            tasks = [process_image(session, url, executor) for url in urls]
            results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    print(f"Processed {len(results)} images in {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    print("Used: AsyncIO (I/O) + ProcessPool (CPU) = Optimal!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

diagrams.title: Picking threads, processes or asyncio
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  start(["What dominates the work?"]) --> q1{"Mostly waiting on I/O?"}
  q1 -->|yes| q2{"Async libraries available and many connections?"}
  q2 -->|yes| asyncio["asyncio — thousands of sockets on one thread"]
  q2 -->|no| threads["Threads — ThreadPoolExecutor around blocking libraries"]
  q1 -->|no| q3{"Pure Python CPU work?"}
  q3 -->|yes| procs["Processes — ProcessPoolExecutor, one per core"]
  q3 -->|"no, C code releases the GIL"| threads2["Threads are fine — numpy, hashing, compression"]
  asyncio --> mix["Mixed workload: asyncio plus run_in_executor for the blocking or CPU parts"]
  threads --> mix
  procs --> mix
diagrams.explain: Answer two questions: *is the work waiting or computing?* and *are the libraries async-capable?* Waiting + async libraries → asyncio; waiting + blocking libraries → threads; pure-Python computing → processes. Real services are usually mixed, so the common production shape is an asyncio core that pushes blocking or CPU-heavy calls to an executor.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Gotchas
sections.body:
- **GIL misconception**: "Threads are useless in Python" — FALSE for I/O-bound work
- **Wrong tool choice**: Using multiprocessing for I/O wastes resources
- **Blocking in async**: Using `time.sleep()` instead of `await asyncio.sleep()` blocks the event loop
- **Shared state**: Assuming GIL makes code thread-safe (it doesn't!)
- **Overhead ignorance**: Processes have high startup cost, not suitable for small tasks
- **Debug complexity**: Concurrent bugs are notoriously hard to reproduce

sections.title: Performance Notes
sections.body:
| Aspect          | Threading | Multiprocessing | AsyncIO  |
| --------------- | --------- | --------------- | -------- |
| Memory per unit | ~8KB      | ~30MB           | ~1KB     |
| Startup time    | ~1ms      | ~100ms          | ~0.1ms   |
| Context switch  | ~10μs     | N/A (OS)        | ~1μs     |
| Max concurrent  | ~1000     | ~100            | ~100,000 |
| GIL impact      | Yes       | No              | Yes      |
